subject: AI & Agents
title: TD-Gammon: The Backgammon Surprise
description: A micro-lesson that makes TD-Gammon: The Backgammon Surprise usable.

hook.text: In 1992, an AI taught itself backgammon by playing a million games against itself. It rivaled world champions.

buildup.text: Gerald Tesauro built TD-Gammon using temporal difference learning — a reinforcement learning technique.

discovery.text: The AI developed strategies that contradicted conventional wisdom — and turned out to be better.

twist.text: Human backgammon champions adopted the AI's strategies. The student became the teacher.

climax.text: TD-Gammon proved self-play could discover superhuman strategies decades before AlphaGo.

punchline.text: Play yourself a million times and you learn moves no one ever imagined.

quiz.question: What was remarkable about TD-Gammon's playing strategies?
options: It developed strategies that contradicted and surpassed conventional wisdom
It perfectly copied human championship games
It could only play one move per game

details.summary: In the early 1990s, TD-Gammon used a neural network and reinforcement learning to play backgammon at world-class level. It was one of the first demonstrations that neural networks could master complex games.
details.whyItMatters: TD-Gammon proved neural networks plus self-play could achieve expert-level performance decades before AlphaGo. It was a foundational milestone that inspired later breakthroughs in game-playing AI.
takeaways: TD-Gammon reached world-class backgammon play in the 1990s
It used temporal difference learning and neural networks
The approach foreshadowed modern reinforcement learning successes

faq.question: Why was TD-Gammon significant for AI history?
faq.answer: It demonstrated that neural networks combined with self-play could master a complex game. Created by Gerald Tesauro at IBM, it was a key early proof that reinforcement learning had real potential.

faq.question: How did TD-Gammon compare to later game-playing AI?
faq.answer: TD-Gammon used similar principles to what AlphaGo would apply decades later: neural networks evaluating positions and learning from self-play. It was a pioneer in the approach that ultimately conquered Go.
